title: Disney and the NFL Launch Limited-Edition Mickey & Friends Merch Ahead of Super Bowl LXI
description:
Mickey & Friends are getting ready to head to Super Bowl LXI with a new lineup of limited-edition merchandise.

	Through their collaboration with th
body:
Mickey & Friends are getting ready to head to Super Bowl LXI with a new lineup of limited-edition merchandise.

	Through their collaboration with the NFL, Disney launched three new collections on Thursday: Disney x Champion, Disney x FOCO and Disney Pinnacle by Dapper Labs.

	Featuring an array of T-shirts and crewnecks, the Disney x Champion collaboration celebrates the upcoming Super Bowl alongside the Disney Pinnacle by Dapper Labs launch, which features Mickey & Friends Super Bowl LXI digital pin packs. With merchandise for all 32 teams, the Disney x FOCO partnership lets fans show off their favorite NFL teams alongside Mickey & Friends with plush, clip-on plush, bobbleheads, figurines and clear stadium bags.


		

						
			
	

					HoldenKudlaPhotography
	
					
		

										LIMITED-EDITION						

					Disney x Champion 		

		
	

	“Sports is a growing area for Disney Consumer Products, reaching highly engaged audiences and sitting at the center of culture,” Paul Gitter, the executive vice president of global licensing at Disney Consumer Products, said in a statement. “As ESPN brings fans along the road to Super Bowl LXI, these products give them another way to connect with the teams, athletes and stories they love, while Mickey & Friends bring a uniquely Disney expression to the heart of NFL culture.”

	As the football season advances closer to Super Bowl LXI, the Disney and NFL collection, which first debuted in August, will continue to release product drops inspired by Mickey and Friends from Crocs, Just Play, New Era, WinCraft and more from Champion.

	“The NFL and Disney are embarking on one of the most exciting chapters in our shared history,” said Casey Collins, the senior vice president of consumer products and licensing at the NFL. “With new products already in the market and more to come in the lead up to Super Bowl LXI on Disney’s networks and platforms, there is no better time to be a fan of these two iconic brands.”


	This year marks the 40th anniversary of “Disney’s Super Bowl What’s Next” campaign, which will be celebrated by the Super Bowl airing on ESPN and ABC and streaming on Disney+ for the first time.

schema.headline: Disney and the NFL Launch Limited-Edition Mickey & Friends Merch Ahead of Super Bowl LXI

title: ‘Harry Potter’ Agent The Blair Partnership Taps Merlin’s Will Obbard, Amazon’s Alex Flanagan for Senior Roles as It Eyes New Growth Phase (EXCLUSIVE)
description: “Harry Potter” agent The Blair Partnership has appointed Will Obbard and Alex Flanagan to senior roles as the company eyes a new phase of growth.
body:
“Harry Potter” agent The Blair Partnership has appointed Will Obbard and Alex Flanagan to senior roles as the company eyes a new phase of growth.

	“I’m delighted to welcome Alex and Will to The Blair Partnership,” said Neil Blair, founding partner of The Blair Partnership. “Both bring exceptional experience in their respective fields and their appointments significantly strengthen our talented leadership team as we look to the next phase of the business and growth. Together, they bring complementary expertise that will help us delight our clients, turbo charge our intellectual property and harness new opportunities for growth and innovation.”
	

	Obbard joins from theme park operator Merlin Entertainments, where he was VP of partnerships. He will lead TBP’s five-year growth strategy focusing on new revenue streams via partnerships, new franchises, mergers and acquisitions. He will also seek out new revenue opportunities for existing clients and IP.

	Obbard spent over 12 years at Merlin and before that worked in strategy and M&A at KPMG. 

	“I’m thrilled to be joining The Blair Partnership at such an exciting point in its development,” said Obbard, who is an official World Book Day trustee. “The group has an exceptional portfolio of clients and intellectual property, alongside significant opportunities to build new partnerships and revenue streams. I’m looking forward to working with the team to deliver on its ambitious growth strategy.”

	Flanagan, who has extensive entertainment, music, digital media and licensing experience, was appointed group general counsel earlier this year. She joins after three and a half years in Amazon’s global media and entertainment division where she represented Amazon Music and Prime Video in complex licensing agreements with music rights holders and public policy and regulatory matters.
	

	Prior to Amazon, Flanagan was VP for global digital legal and business affairs at Universal Music Group and head of legal for UMG’s independent artist distribution platform Spinnup.

	She said: “I’m thrilled to be joining The Blair Partnership at such an exciting time for the business. The combination of world-class literary talent, distinctive intellectual property and growing entertainment opportunities creates huge potential to build on its success and unlock new avenues for growth. I’m looking forward to being part of that journey.”

	As well as “Harry Potter,” which is set to debut a highly-anticipated new screen version on HBO and HBO Max this Christmas, The Blair Partnership represents British family classic brands including The Wombles and the world of Neverland from “Peter Pan.” The company offers full-service entertainment representation for authors, creators and IP.

schema.headline: ‘Harry Potter’ Agent The Blair Partnership Taps Merlin’s Will Obbard, Amazon’s Alex Flanagan for Senior Roles as It Eyes New Growth Phase (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Brian Gleeson, Colm Meaney, Alex Murphy and Aidan Gillen to Star in ‘Paddy Power’ Film Charting Rise of Irish Gambling Giant (EXCLUSIVE)
description: The story of how a small Dublin bookmaker turned into one of the world’s most recognizable betting companies is being made into a feature film, wit
body:
The story of how a small Dublin bookmaker turned into one of the world’s most recognizable betting companies is being made into a feature film, with a quartet of Irish actors attached to star. 

	Brian Gleeson (“Under Salt Marsh,” “Logan Lucky”), Colm Meaney (“Law Abiding Citizen,” “Layer Cake”), Alex Murphy (“Saipan,” “The Young Offenders”) and Aidan Gillen (“Game of Thrones,” “Queer as Folk”) are set to lead the cast of “Paddy Power,” with Matt Lipsey (“Ted Lasso,” “Inside No.9”) tapped to direct.
	

	The film, from Irish media production company Playhouse Studios, is based on award-winning investigative journalist Aaron Rogan’s acclaimed “Punters: How Paddy Power Bet Billions and Changed Gambling Forever,” charting the rise of the infamous gambling giant. Long-time writing duo Dale Longmore and John Quinn (“Bump”) will adapt Rogan’s book and pen the script with Brian Durnin (“Spilt Milk”).

	As per the synopsis, “Paddy Power” will recount the “crazy true story of how one man bet big on brash advertising and brought online gambling — and addiction — to every corner of the globe.” It adds: “An inherently Irish origin story, it claws open the lid of how a few chancers changed the world as we know it, destroying hundreds of thousands of people’s lives forever.”

	The film marks a significant milestone for Playhouse Studios as it unveils the first title from its original scripted slate. 

	“’Paddy Power’ stood out immediately as a story with real scale, authentic dark humour, grit and tenacity. You could not make up this incredible story,” said Playhouse CEO Peggy Cafferty. “Aaron Rogan’s voice made the book such an easy, engaging read and we feel the writing team captured the adaptation brilliantly. This is the extraordinary rise of one company that refused to play by the rules and set out on a path of ambition, risk and consequence. They stepped outside the norms of marketing with brilliant twists and always with wit. We are thrilled with this exceptional creative team and cast, this is a fearless production and a narrative that resonates with audiences far beyond Ireland — everyone loves a great, true story that’s as dramatic as fiction.”
	

	Added Rogan: “I’m delighted that Peggy and the team at Playhouse see the same value in the Paddy Power story that I have since I started reporting on them a decade ago. It’s an Irish story with global appeal and the growth of the gambling industry in the U.S. in recent years makes this adaptation all the more timely.”

	Playhouse Studios also recently financed Underground Films and Rocliffe Productions’ “Lemonade,” starring Barry Keoghan, which world premiered at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. With the recent opening of its Playhouse Post base in London’s Soho and a Belfast office, the expansion forms part of Playhouse Studios’ wider strategy to build an integrated production ecosystem across the U.K. and Ireland, spanning development, financing, production and post-production.

schema.headline: Brian Gleeson, Colm Meaney, Alex Murphy and Aidan Gillen to Star in ‘Paddy Power’ Film Charting Rise of Irish Gambling Giant (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Ji.hlava New Visions Award Winner Karim Akalay Mixes Magic With ‘Anti-Social Realism’ in ‘6TM’: ‘It’s About Collective Strength Rather Than One Hero’
description: Karim Akalay’s “6TM” won the New Visions Award for the most promising European project at Ji.hlava Documentary Film Festival. Variety spoke to Akal
body:
Karim Akalay’s “6TM” won the New Visions Award for the most promising European project at Ji.hlava Documentary Film Festival. Variety spoke to Akalay at the festival. 

	Set during a scorching summer at Brussels’ largest housing estate, Cité Modèle, the story follows three intertwining narratives within one family. 

	Two kids chase a magic key to prevent their friend, who uses a wheelchair, from being forced out due to broken elevators. A teenage girl assembles a team of misfits to compete in a soccer tournament. A mother rallies her neighbors to uncover who stole the rain.
	

	The team describes it as a “Belgian family comedy in three chapters, rooted in magic realism and the resilience of a community.”

	“Cité Modèle, one of the biggest and most symbolic housing estate in Brussels, [is] where I was born,” Akalay says. “Each of these characters faces a very real problem, and each finds a very magical solution.”

	Its title is a French wordplay, he explains. 

	“6T, pronounced ‘six-T,’ sounds like ‘cité,’ which means housing estate. The ‘m’ stands for ‘modèle.’ So ‘6TM’ simply means Cité Modèle, but it’s more than just an abbreviation. It’s the language of the people who live there. Writing it that way is how residents make the place their own. The film’s title comes from within the neighborhood, just like its stories.”

	Having multiple protagonists was an obvious choice.

	“A housing estate is never just one person’s story. In the Cité, the lives of the kids, teenagers and parents are all connected. By following three generations of one family, I could show how the entire community resists in their own way.”
	

	He adds: “It’s a film about collective strength rather than one hero.”

	Akalay always wanted to combine magic realism with a realistic setting.

	“Belgium has a strong tradition of social realism, with the Dardenne brothers as its best-known example. These are important films, but they often portray people like my neighbors only through hardship. I wanted to do the opposite, a kind of ‘anti-social realism,’” he says.

	“The problems in ‘6TM’ are real: broken elevators, heat, people being pushed out. But the way the characters respond is joyful, funny and inventive. Magic – and a touch of manga – is how I show their imagination and strength.”

	Producers Walid Bekhti and Hanoulia Salamé agree: “For us, the realism is what makes the magic credible. The film is shot on location with non-professional actors and real stories from the neighborhood, so the fantasy never feels like an escape. It feels like something the community creates itself,” they said in a joint statement.

	It’s also a family film in the full sense of the word.

	“Children and teenagers can enjoy the adventure, and adults will recognize the social reality behind it. We also think it speaks to audiences who rarely see neighborhoods like the Cité Modèle on screen, except in dramas,” they add.

	“We want them to laugh and to feel proud. Broadcasters are essential in reaching that audience, and the work of RTBF, Proximus and BeTV in supporting new talents matters a lot.”

	Akalay also considers young people when envisioning his target audience.

	“In Belgium and in France, Gen Z is angry, and they show it. But they don’t only protest: they create too,” he says.

	“They make videos, music and images, and they transform their anger into something inventive and often very funny. That’s exactly the energy of the characters in ‘6TM.’ I want this generation to recognize itself in the film.”

	“6TM” is currently in development, with filming planned for July 2027. It is produced by Walid Bekhti and Hanoulia Salamé for Centre Vidéo de Bruxelles (Belgium) with support from the Wallonia-Brussels Federation, Groupe Ouest and the New Dawn Fund.

schema.headline: Ji.hlava New Visions Award Winner Karim Akalay Mixes Magic With ‘Anti-Social Realism’ in ‘6TM’: ‘It’s About Collective Strength Rather Than One Hero’

title: ‘The Debut’ to Open Marrakech Film Festival, With ‘Artificial’ and ‘Paper Tiger’ Among Gala Screenings
description: Jesse Eisenberg’s “The Debut,” starring Julianne Moore as a shy housewife who is cast in a community theater musical and transforms into a zealous
body:
Jesse Eisenberg’s “The Debut,” starring Julianne Moore as a shy housewife who is cast in a community theater musical and transforms into a zealous Method actor, has been set as the opening film of the 23rd Marrakech International Film Festival.

	Eisenberg and Moore are both expected to be on hand for the out-of-competition gala. 

	The fest, running from Nov. 20-28, will also feature the regional premiere of Luca Guadagnino’s “Artificial,” which traces the rise of OpenAI founder Sam Altman (played by Andrew Garfield). Guadagnino is a Marrakech regular, as is James Gray, who will also be returning with his crime thriller “Paper Tiger” starring Adam Driver and Miles Teller.
	

	Other Marrakech gala screenings include two world premieres: Brazilian director Fellipe Barbosa’s “Leila et la nuit,” inspired by the life of Moroccan photographer Leila Alaoui and starring Roschdy Zem and Marina Foïs; and Egyptian helmer Omar Hilal’s “His Weakest Creatures,” which pairs Egyptian stars Ahmed Helmy and Hend Sabry together on screen for the first time.

	John Turturro will be making the trek to present Noah Segan’s “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” in which the actor delivers a standout performance as an aging pickpocket contending with the contemporary world. The section also includes Laïla Marrakchi’s “Strawberries,” which has been selected as Morocco’s Oscars entry and follows a group of Moroccan seasonal laborers hired to pick strawberries in Spain who decide to stand up to their abusive employers.

	The Official Competition showcases new talent in world cinema with 14 first and second feature films competing for the Étoile d’Or, awarded by a jury headed by actor Marion Cotillard.
	

	Three titles in the competition are world premieres: Sahara-set drama “Alkebulan,” by Moroccan director Yassine Marco Marroccu; Iranian-Norwegian filmmaker Farzad Samsami’s “Waves of Silence,” a Morocco-set drama about migrant shipwrecks; and “Cairo Shadows,” a political thriller set in the Coptic Christian community in Egypt, directed by Rani Massalha e Salem Massalha.

	Marrakech competition entries that have surfaced elsewhere, and will be having their regional premiers comprise Marie-Clémentine Dusabejambo’s post-genocide drama “Ben’imana,” that premiered in Un Certain Regard at Cannes; Palestinian director Abdallah Alkhatib’s “Chronicles From the Siege” depicting desperation of Palestinian lives on the front lines; Rafiki Fariala’s Cannes standout title “Congo Boy” about the musical dreams of a young Congolese refugee; and Lebanese director Rami Kodeih’s bank-heist thriller “Furies” that delves into the Lebanese economic crisis.

	The Horizons section featuring 21 films “that demonstrate the vitality and diversity of world cinema,” as the festival put it, including several titles that have won top honors at Cannes and Venice, will showcase the latest works by top global auteurs, including Ryusuke Hamaguchi “All of a Sudden”; Cristian Mungiu “Fjord”; Pawel Pawlikowski (“Fatherland”); Hirokazu Kore-eda (“Look Back”); and Nanni Moretti (“It Happened One Night”). Arab cinema will be featured in the section with Egyptian director Mohammed Hammad’s psychological thriller “Safe Exit”; Sara Ishaq’s Yemen-set “The Station,” and Gaza-set doc “Citizen Osama,” directed by Ahmed Hassouna.

	The Moroccan Panorama section will feature six works and open with Tala Hadid’s “Bardi,” about a traveling brotherhood of horsemen and theit journey across Morocco. A total of 11 Moroccan films are sprinkled across the fest’s various sections, in addition to three films shot in Morocco.

schema.headline: ‘The Debut’ to Open Marrakech Film Festival, With ‘Artificial’ and ‘Paper Tiger’ Among Gala Screenings

title: Hawai’i International Film Festival Crowns ‘We Are Aliens’ as Ke Huy Quan, Sung Kang Receive Honors (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Japanese director Kadowaki Kōhei’s animated feature “We Are Aliens” has won the Kau Ka Hōkū (Shooting Star) Award at the 46th Hawai’i International
body:
Japanese director Kadowaki Kōhei’s animated feature “We Are Aliens” has won the Kau Ka Hōkū (Shooting Star) Award at the 46th Hawai’i International Film Festival, which handed out its jury prizes at an awards reception at the Halekulani Hotel in Waikīkī on Nov. 1.

	Presented by Hawaiian Airlines, the prize is reserved for an international filmmaker’s first or second feature. Festival programmers pick the nominees, fiction and nonfiction alike, and an international jury chooses the winner. “We Are Aliens,” which had its world premiere at Cannes, charts a childhood friendship that breaks apart over what looks like a small incident, following the fallout over three decades.
	

	“For giving childhood a physical presence through hand-drawn animation, rotoscoping and dialogue that feels overheard, and for capturing the cruelty children learn from one another and what memory eventually makes of it, we unanimously give Kadowaki Kōhei’s ‘We Are Aliens’ the Kau Ka Hōkū Award,” the jury said. “We offer our highest praise for an emotional force that should not be allowed in a first feature.”

	The jurors were Samuel Jamier, president of the New York Asian Film Festival; Jesse Hawthorne Ficks, film critic and San Francisco Bay Guardian producer; and Mia Lee Vicino, film journalist and former West Coast editor of Letterboxd. They also handed an honorable mention to “The Seoul Guardians.”

	Zilla Barbosa’s “Making the Line” was named best Made in Hawai’i feature. “The film thoughtfully captures an intense emotional journey often kept behind-the-scenes and celebrates the grit, determination and perseverance required to uphold Hawaiian excellence,” the jury said, adding that it “marks a triumphant debut for a filmmaker from Hilo, Hawaii, whose work in music and radio has long served this community.”
	

	Justyn Ah Chong’s “The Man and the Tree” picked up two prizes. It won best Made in Hawai’i short, which puts it in line for Oscar qualification, and also took the Pacific Award’s short film honor, a category added this year for the first time. The Made in Hawai’i jury said the narrative short depicts “the beauty and weight of an entire life cycle and does so while staying true to a Native Hawaiian perspective.”

	Aukai Lagiri’s “Kukulu” received an honorable mention in the Made in Hawai’i short category, while Ty Sanga’s “Lahaina: Voices of Change” earned honorable mentions from both the Made in Hawai’i and Pacific Award juries.

	The Made in Hawai’i jury comprised Michelle Sugihara, executive director and CEO of the Coalition of Asian Pacifics in Entertainment (CAPE); Taylour Chang, Bishop Museum’s director of public programs and community engagement; and producer and location manager Kent Matsuoka. Now in its 10th year, the strand is backed by the Nichols Family Fund and the Hawai’i Film Office, and its titles can be programmed on Hawaiian Airlines flights.

	Jordan Manley’s “The Navigator” won the Pacific Award for best feature, which HIFF presents with Pacific Islanders in Communications. “At the heart of this film is the indigenous transmission of knowledge, from one generation to the next. It is about the magic we seek, but perhaps do not always find,” the jury said. Its members were Samoan-born New Zealand filmmaker Miki Magasiva; Native Hawaiian academic, curator and lawyer Noelle Kahanu; and independent producer Averie Joy Maikalima O Makua Huffine.

	The HIFF Best Short Film Award, presented by Hawaiian Airlines and Oscar-qualifying for international shorts, went to Fraser Pemberton and William Jaka’s Australian drama-thriller “Faceless.” It centers on a Warlpiri man living three parallel lives along the Birrarung-Ga (Yarra River) in Naarm (Melbourne).

	“Every one of us arrived at the same word: wow. A unanimous wow,” the jury said. “It’s a film that keeps unfolding after it ends.” The panel included screenwriter and producer Philip W. Chung; Christine Yi, president of Gold House Studios and general manager of Gold House Labs; and Sarah Fang, manager of the Doris Duke Theatre and programmer at the Honolulu Museum of Art.
	

	Zou Jing’s “A Girl Unknown” (China) took the Netpac/USA Award from a field of 12 nominees. HIFF is the sole U.S. festival permitted to hand out the Network for the Promotion of Asian-Pacific Cinema prize, which is also given at Berlin, Cannes, Venice, Toronto, Rotterdam and Busan, among others. The jury called the film a “patient and carefully layered human story in which a young woman finds a way to survive oppression and seek her own future.”

	Its jurors were Duncan Caillard, a Melbourne-based film researcher and critic who lectures in global creative industries at the University of Melbourne; Libby Hakaraia, head of Māoriland Films; and Therese Hayes, a film festival consultant and Netpac USA member.

	“This year’s winners reflect the strength and diversity of cinematic storytelling today, here in Hawai’i and across the region,” said Jean H. Lee, the festival’s executive director. “We are thankful to our distinguished jurors for their careful consideration and proud of the quality of films in this year’s festival.”

	Festival audiences voted Sung Kang’s “Drifter” favorite narrative feature, Frank W. Chen’s Taiwanese documentary “Beyond the Smiles: Yani Tseng” favorite documentary and Lauren Luke’s “Sons Are Not Earthbound” favorite short. The Audience Awards are presented by Hawai’i News Now.

	Kang was also among the honorees feted at the HIFF Honoree Gala in the Halekulani Ballroom on Oct. 29, hosted by Sisa Grey (“Chief of War,” “Star Wars: Skeleton Crew,” “Fallout”). Best known as Han in “The Fast & the Furious” franchise, Kang received the Halekulani Maverick Award. He wrote, directed, produced and stars in “Drifter,” in which a loner working as a janitor finds his way back, and a community, through competitive drifting.

	Ke Huy Quan received the Halekulani Golden Maile Career Achievement Award. Quan, who began his career as Short Round in “Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom” and Data in “The Goonies,” stepped back from acting, taking stunt choreography and behind-the-scenes jobs, before his comeback in “Everything Everywhere All at Once,” which won him the Oscar for his turn as Waymond. He most recently voiced Gary De’Snake in Disney’s “Zootopia 2,” a role he will reprise in “Zootopia 3,” and published his memoir “Never Say Die” in September.
	

	Master navigator Nainoa Thompson, CEO of the Polynesian Voyaging Society, was given the Halekulani Legacy Award. In 1980, he guided a voyaging canoe from Hawai’i to Tahiti with no modern instruments, the first Native Hawaiian to do so in centuries.

	Tongan and New Zealand actor Luciane Buchanan (“The Night Agent,” “Chief of War,” “Evil Dead Burn”) took the Halekulani New Vanguard Award. Native Hawaiian screenwriter Bryson Chun, whose credits include “Doogie Kamealoha, M.D.” and “Moana 2,” received the Leanne K. Ferrer Trailblazer Award, presented by Pacific Islanders in Communications.

	Among those at the gala were Stephy Tang, this year’s Spotlight on Hong Kong artist, along with Josie Ho, Daniel Dae Kim and director Bao Nguyen.

	HIFF46 opened Oct. 21 at the Hawaii Theatre. After Honolulu, the festival moves to Kapolei, Maui, Moloka’i, Hawai’i Island and Lāna’i for screenings running Nov. 3–15.

	HIFF46 WINNERS

	Kau Ka Hōkū Award“We Are Aliens” (Japan)Director: Kadowaki KōheiHonorable Mention: “The Seoul Guardians”

	Pacific Award – Feature“The Navigator” (U.S.)Director: Jordan Manley

	Pacific Award – Short“The Man and the Tree” (U.S.)Director: Justyn Ah Chong

	Best Made in Hawai’i Feature“Making the Line”Director: Zilla Barbosa

	Best Made in Hawai’i Short“The Man and the Tree”Director: Justyn Ah Chong

	Made in Hawai’i Short – Honorable Mention“Kukulu”Director: Aukai Lagiri

	Made in Hawai’i and Pacific Award – Honorable Mention“Lahaina: Voices of Change”Director: Ty Sanga

	HIFF Best Short Film Award“Faceless” (Australia)Directors: Fraser Pemberton, William Jaka

	Netpac Award“A Girl Unknown” (China)Director: Zou Jing

	Audience Award – Favorite Narrative Feature“Drifter” (U.S.)Director: Sung Kang

	Audience Award – Favorite Documentary“Beyond the Smiles: Yani Tseng” (Taiwan)Director: Frank W. Chen

	Audience Award – Favorite Short“Sons Are Not Earthbound” (U.S.)Director: Lauren Luke

	Halekulani Golden Maile Career Achievement AwardKe Huy Quan

title: Ukraine-Set Drama About a Trans Man Barred From Fleeing War, ‘I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming,’ Wins Tokyo’s Ethical Film Award
description: German director and screenwriter Isabelle Stever’s “I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming” has won the Tokyo International Film Festival’s Ethical Film Award.
body:
German director and screenwriter Isabelle Stever’s “I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming” has won the Tokyo International Film Festival’s Ethical Film Award.

	The award, set up in 2023 with sponsor Sumitomo Corporation, highlights films that shed light on issues such as the environment, poverty and discrimination. A jury picks the winner from three nominees drawn from the festival lineup.


	Actor Isomura Hayato, a two-time Japan Academy Film Prize winner who runs the Shizuoka Film Festival in his hometown, headed this year’s jury. He was joined by three members of the festival’s student PR team. The other nominees were Brazil’s “Amadeo and the Hypothetical New World,” directed by Brenda Lígia and Edu Felistoque, and Australia’s “Time and Tide,” directed by Vee Shi.
	

	Stever’s film, a Germany-Ukraine co-production, opens in Kyiv at the end of 2021, months before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Oleh, a trans man, tries to leave the country to escape the coming war but is barred because of the gender listed on his documents. He stays behind with his partner, Olya, and the couple struggle to hold on to their relationship and their sense of self as the bombing draws closer.

	Stever’s earlier films have had their premieres at the Berlinale and at festivals in Toronto, Locarno and Busan. She worked on her two most recent features with her wife, the Ukrainian novelist and screenwriter Anna Melikova.

	Isomura said the jury rated the film highly for taking on gender against the backdrop of the current war between Russia and Ukraine. The film follows a couple swept up in that war whose identity, sense of purpose and values are shaken and denied, he said, and asks how people can go on living under those conditions. He said the jurors chose it in the hope that many people would see it and take some time to reflect.
	

	Stever, who could not travel to Tokyo, accepted the award in a video message recorded during a break from teaching at a film school. “Queer is not only referring to LGBTQ+. It is, as well, referring to something that is not normalized,” she said. “And we all know if everything would be normalized, we would stop breathing.”

	She linked that idea to autocratic regimes, where people must obey set standards and have no other options, and to Ukrainians fighting “so people can still breathe in this country.”

	The festival will send Stever a certificate and a cash prize of JPY200,000 ($1,270) at a later date.

schema.headline: Ukraine-Set Drama About a Trans Man Barred From Fleeing War, ‘I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming,’ Wins Tokyo’s Ethical Film Award

title: Sharjah Film Festival Takeaways: ‘Atlas of the Universe’ Takes Top Prize, Pitching Platform Doubles and Audience Award Debuts
description: The 13th Sharjah Intl. Film Festival for Children and Youth wrapped Sunday with Paul Negoescu’s “Atlas of the Universe” taking best feature film an
body:
The 13th Sharjah Intl. Film Festival for Children and Youth wrapped Sunday with Paul Negoescu’s “Atlas of the Universe” taking best feature film and Celia Catunda’s “My Grandfather Is a Nihonjin” winning best animated feature.

	The jury described “Atlas of the Universe,” a Romanian-Bulgarian coming-of-age drama about a 10-year-old boy whose errand to buy school shoes becomes a journey toward independence, as “the essence of this festival.” Brazilian animation “My Grandfather Is a Nihonjin,” about a Japanese-Brazilian boy exploring his family history and cultural identity, was recognized for its treatment of tradition and “the difficulty of starting a new life in a foreign place.”
	

	Areej Alghamdi’s Saudi film “The Path of Memory, Between the Lands of Jasmine and Basil,” which explores cultural memory and heritage through a young girl and her mother, won best documentary. Abdulrahman Al Madani’s Emirati film “Oug,” about a childless couple confronting family pressure and gendered blame surrounding infertility, took best Arabic short.

	Shweta Parakh and Rakesh E Nair’s “Little Big Dreams” won best international short. The film follows a girl in Ladakh, India, who uses a wheelchair and is determined to pursue her education and be seen with “pride rather than pity.” The jury praised it for portraying “resilience, friendship and the power of the human spirit.”

	Thai narrative feature “Gohan,” directed by Chayanop Bunprakob, Baz Poonpiriya and Atta Hemwadee, won the festival’s inaugural Audience Award. The film, which follows a stray dog through the lives of three owners over more than a decade, also received a special mention from the feature film jury.
	

	Other winners included South Korea’s “The Monster” for best child and youth-made film, and “Raeda” for best student-made short. “Fellow” won best student short animation and “The Great Dreamscape” was named best animation short. Saudi documentary “Marjooj” received a special mention.

	The festival screened 71 films from 38 countries, selected from 1,802 submissions from 72 countries, with Italy serving as Country of Honor.

	Beyond the prizes, this year’s edition reflected SIFF’s growing focus on industry development, regional connections and even greater participation from its young audiences.

	Here are five takeaways from this year’s festival.

	SIFF Is Building a Pipeline, Not Just a Festival

	SIFF continued to expand the ways young people can participate beyond watching films, with programs introducing them to different parts of the industry.

	Its Junior Jurors program puts young participants on festival juries, while the Festival Ambassadors program gives them experience representing and covering the annual event. The Industry Hub connects emerging filmmakers with established professionals through panels, workshops and other activities.

	The Industry Hub also addressed how festivals make selection decisions. During one panel, programmers discussed how acceptance or rejection is not necessarily a verdict on quality, with decisions shaped by lineup balance, geography and audience.

	“For those who do want to pursue filmmaking, we want SIFF to remain part of their journey, from their first experience of cinema to their first professional opportunities,” festival director Sheikha Jawaher bint Abdullah Al Qasimi told Variety ahead of the festival.

	The Pitching Platform Is Growing Into a Bigger Industry Tool

	SIFF doubled its pitching platform in its second year, selecting six projects compared with three in 2025.

	Rather than offering a cash prize, the platform connects filmmakers with industry professionals who could provide financing, production support or other forms of collaboration. The projects ranged from completed screenplays seeking financing to films looking for post-production support and international partners.

	Khalid Al Mahmoud’s “The Mangrove House” offered an early example of its potential. The Emirati filmmaker pitched the project at the platform’s inaugural edition in 2025 while seeking post-production support. FANN – Media Discovery Platform, SIFF’s parent organization, later backed the film, which returned this year to open the festival with its world premiere.
	

	Regional Exchange Is Starting With the Next Generation

	SIFF is also using its youth programs to build connections across the region. Egyptian actors Ali Beialy, 12, and Retal Abdelaziz, 15, were among the young participants invited to Sharjah as junior jurors this year.

	The pair took part in jury duties, introduced films and covered festival events. For Beialy, the experience changed how he watched films, pushing him to consider cinematography, lighting and directing alongside story.

	“We all come from different backgrounds, but we share the same interest, which gives us a great opportunity to learn from each other and introduce our own visions, cultures and experiences,” he told Variety.

	Abdelaziz, who watches older films to study different aspects of acting and filmmaking, said representing Egypt came with a sense of responsibility. “I am proud to represent my country, Egypt, and I see the exchange of ideas and experiences between countries as very important,” she said.

	That regional exchange extends elsewhere at SIFF. This year’s pitching platform brought together projects from the UAE, Oman and the Palestinian diaspora in the U.S., while the competition includes a dedicated section for Arabic short films.

	Emirati Filmmakers Want an Ecosystem That Can Sustain Them

	The only two Emirati films in competition raised a persistent question surrounding the country’s film sector and how to build an infrastructure that allows local filmmakers to keep working.

	Al Mahmoud’s “The Mangrove House” and Al Madani’s “Oug” draw from distinctly local experiences, but their directors pointed to continuing challenges around financing, production support, distribution and reaching audiences.

	The discussion comes as the UAE’s film landscape shifts, with the Dubai Intl. Film Festival set to return in December 2027 after a decade-long hiatus.

	During SIFF, FANN signed a memorandum of understanding with the UAE’s National Media Authority covering film screening procedures, media coordination, regulatory procedures, training and technical support. The federal body also became an official supporting partner of the festival.

	For a festival increasingly focused on what happens to filmmakers beyond workshops and screenings, the agreement brings a federal media partner into a local film industry that directors say still has room to grow.
	

	For the First Time, Audiences Get a Vote

	SIFF introduced its first Audience Award this year, giving festivalgoers a direct say in the prizes. After each screening, audiences could scan a QR code to rate the film.

	Thai feature “Gohan,” which had its Middle East premiere as one of the festival’s Green Carpet screenings, won the inaugural award.

	“We wanted to give them a greater role in the festival and make their opinions count,” Huda Al Harmoudi, deputy director of FANN, told Variety. “The response has been very positive, and we’re pleased to see audiences taking part.”

schema.headline: Sharjah Film Festival Takeaways: ‘Atlas of the Universe’ Takes Top Prize, Pitching Platform Doubles and Audience Award Debuts

title: Palestinian-Jordanian Filmmaker Darin J. Sallam on the Backlash to ‘Farha’: ‘I Never Regretted It’
description: Palestinian-Jordanian filmmaker Darin J. Sallam has no regrets about making “Farha,” her debut feature about a Palestinian girl coming of age durin
body:
Palestinian-Jordanian filmmaker Darin J. Sallam has no regrets about making “Farha,” her debut feature about a Palestinian girl coming of age during the Nakba, the mass displacement and dispossession of Palestinians surrounding the creation of the state of Israel in 1948. The film sparked controversy that Sallam was warned could derail her career before it had properly begun.

	“I never questioned that decision or regretted it for a moment,” Sallam tells Variety from UAE, where she is serving as a member of the narrative features jury at the 13th Sharjah Intl. Festival for Children and Youth. “Everything that went into bringing the film to life was worth it, and its impact continues to resonate to this day.”
	

	“Farha” was inspired by the story of a Palestinian refugee, passed down to Sallam through her mother. The film premiered at the Toronto Film Festival in 2021, was later selected as Jordan’s submission for the international feature Oscar and subsequently streamed globally on Netflix.

	Its Netflix release prompted a fierce backlash, particularly over a scene depicting Israeli soldiers killing a Palestinian family. Israeli officials publicly condemned the film, while Sallam and others involved with it faced harassment and online abuse. Sallam has also been unable to travel to Palestine since the film’s release.

	The warnings rolled in even before the film was shot. “I always knew in my heart that choosing ‘Farha’ as my debut feature film would be an experience unlike anything I had encountered before or will encounter in the future,” she says.
	

	For Sallam, the film grew out of a broader conviction that history is most powerful when experienced through individual lives. “Personal stories are often the most powerful way to understand history and society,” she explains. “Behind every historical event, there are individual lives, emotions, struggles and dreams that deserve to be heard.”

	She is particularly drawn to women’s stories because, she says, so many of their experiences have been “overlooked, silenced or left out of the historical narrative.”

	In “Farha,” that meant filtering the collective experience of the Nakba through the perspective of one young girl. Sallam sees personal and collective memory as inseparable, with Farha’s journey distilling an event that transformed thousands of lives into an experience audiences could encounter through a single character.

	“If cinema is not personal, it risks becoming nothing more than slogans and history lessons,” Sallam argues. “Cinema needs to emerge from a genuine human experience, from something deeply felt and lived. Only then can it move beyond delivering messages and become something that truly touches people, challenges them and stays with them.”

	Sallam is again turning toward women and history with “Churching of Women,” her second feature. Set in the Levant, encompassing present-day Palestine, Lebanon, Syria and Jordan, in 1938, the film follows Fadia, a pioneering female author grieving the loss of her parents who turns to her cousin for support, only to be confined against her will in a mental asylum while he seizes her inheritance. The project took part in the Busan Intl. Film Festival’s Asian Project Market in 2025 where it won the ArteKino International Award. It is now in advanced development and financing.

	It began with an idea about injustice that stayed with Sallam. While she remains committed to telling stories about women whose voices have been suppressed, Sallam says the new film will allow her to explore injustice, grief, women supporting one another and colonial power structures in the region.

	“I’ve always been drawn to certain story setups, and with ‘Churching,’ I’m exploring these on a broader, more complex scale, bringing multiple characters into the mix,” she explains. “It’s a challenge I’m particularly excited about, especially given my love of working with actors.”
	

	The experience of making and releasing “Farha” is inevitably informing the process. Together with her producers, Sallam is considering what they learned from the film’s production, release and distribution, and how that knowledge can serve the journey of “Churching of Women.”

	What it has not done is make her more cautious about the stories she chooses to tell. “If anything, my experience with ‘Farha’ has only strengthened my resolve to bring stories to the world through cinema,” she adds. “I cannot wait to share ‘Churching of Women’ with audiences, along with its unique characters, the world they inhabit and the journey that unfolds around them.”

	That conviction also shapes the way Sallam thinks about younger audiences. Serving on the feature jury at SIFF reinforced her belief that children and adolescents are capable of engaging deeply with cinema.

	“I am always moved by the curiosity and emotional maturity of young audiences,” she says. “They are not spectators to be underestimated because of their age.” Watching children and adolescents engage with films in Sharjah, she adds, has been “absolutely heartwarming.”

title: Jack Lowden Plays Coy About James Bond Rumors: ‘It’s All Very Flattering’ but I’m Not ‘Going to Add to the Noise’
description: Jack Lowden is keeping relatively quiet about the possibility of becoming the next James Bond, even as speculation mounts that the “Slow Horses” st
body:
Jack Lowden is keeping relatively quiet about the possibility of becoming the next James Bond, even as speculation mounts that the “Slow Horses” star is among the frontrunners to replace Daniel Craig as 007.

	In an interview with British GQ, the Scottish actor addressed the ongoing casting rumors, including recent comments from his “Slow Horses” co-star Gary Oldman who publicly backed Lowden for the role:  


	“It’s all very flattering. It’s nice to be mentioned – for any role – and I’m just not really going to add to the noise,” Lowden said. “It’s very nice, and Gary’s a sweetheart – it’s particularly lovely, coming from someone like him. But I don’t really listen to it.”
	

	Lowden, who plays M15 agent River Cartwright opposite Oldman’s Jackson Lamb in the Apple TV spy thriller, suggests that being linked to Bond is almost inevitable for actors of a certain type-cast and age.

	“As a young male actor, generally, the minute you’re not playing a zany artist type, the minute you’re in a suit, people fling it at you,” he said.

	Lowden’s comments arrive as the search for the next Bond reportedly enters its final stages. As Variety reported on Oct. 23, Amazon MGM Studio was preparing to conduct final screen tests for the role, with Lowden and “Masters of the Air” actor Callum Turner believed to be among the contenders. “Challengers” star Josh O’Connor has also reportedly received an offer to test, while other names previously linked to the franchise include Jacob Elordi, Harris Dickinson, Aaron Taylor-Johnson and Paul Mescal. 
	

	Lowden’s name gained particular traction in September after Oldman appeared to suggest that Bond producers had already selected Craig’s successor. Speaking on Canada’s “The Morning Show,” the Oscar winner said Lowden was rumored to be on the shortlist and expressed hope that his co-star would land the part. 

	“They have made their choice, but they have not announced it yet. So my fingers are crossed for Jack,” Oldman said.

	Oldman later clarified his remarks during a Toronto International Film Festival appearance, explaining that he had only heard a rumor that producers had selected an actor from a six-person shortlist, not that Lowden had secured the role. 

	“So I do not know [who has gotten the part], but I’m hoping it’s Jack,” Oldman said. He also pushed back on headlines suggesting he had inside information about the casting process, joking that the coverage made it sound as though he had a direct line to director Denis Villeneuve.

	The next Bond film will mark the franchise’s first installment since Amazon MGM took creative control from longtime custodians Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson in 2025. Villeneuve is attached to direct, with “Peaky Blinders” creator Steven Knight writing the screenplay and Amy Pascal and David Heyman producing. Casting director Nina Gold is overseeing the search for the next 007. 

	Craig last portrayed the British secret agent in 2021’s “No Time to Die,” concluding a five-film run that began with 2006’s “Casino Royale.” An official announcement naming his successor is widely expected before the end of 2026, though Amazon MGM has not confirmed a timeline.

schema.headline: Jack Lowden Plays Coy About James Bond Rumors: ‘It’s All Very Flattering’ but I’m Not ‘Going to Add to the Noise’

title: NJ 5th Grade Teacher, Accused of Having 11-Year-Old Student's Baby, Pleads Guilty
description:

                          Accused of Having 11-Year-Old Student's Baby
body:
NJ Teacher
                          Accused of Having 11-Year-Old Student's Baby
                          Pleads Guilty
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              
                November 1, 2026
                
                            12:48 PM PST
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  November 1, 2026
                                2:39 PM PST
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Laura Caron -- a 36-year-old former 5th grade teacher -- has pleaded guilty to one of the charges against her ... after being accused of sexually assaulting a student and having his baby.
      
    
            Caron -- who was charged in January 2025 -- was accused of abusing her victim as early as 11 years old ... PEOPLE reported.
      
    
            Prosecutors claimed the abuse lasted for 4 years ... and a probable cause affidavit obtained by the outlet claimed she became pregnant with and gave birth to his child.
      

            She was 27 at the time ... he was only 13.
      
    
            Caron pleaded guilty to second-degree endangering the welfare of a child with sexual conduct.
      
    
            As part of her plea ... Caron will not only forfeit her teacher's license, she's set to receive a 5-year sentence, although her sentencing hearing will take place in January.
      
    
            The Cape May County Prosecutor’s Office said in a statement ... "Before Caron serves her State Prison sentence, she will be evaluated at the Adult Diagnostic and Treatment Center at Avenel for classification to determine whether she is deemed repetitive and/or compulsive which could impact her sentence."
      
    
            After serving her sentence ... Caron will also be subject to parole supervision for the rest of her life and have to register as sex offender.

title: Horrifying Audio of Palm Beach Plane Flight Moments Before Crash Revealed
description:
Palm Beach Plane Crash
                          Chilling Audio Revealed
body:
Palm Beach Plane Crash
                          Chilling Audio Revealed
                          'We're Out of Time'
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              
                November 1, 2026
                
                            2:11 PM PST
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  November 1, 2026
                                3:04 PM PST
                                    
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            Audio between air traffic control and a Learjet flight in the moments before it crashed show the plane's crew scrambling to respond as they plummeted in a nose dive.
      
    
            In audio first reported by the California Post, one female crew member yelled ... "Holy f***, we're out of time."
      

            The audio begins with the flight crew telling air traffic controllers that they had experienced moderate turbulence and were dealing with ice.
      
    
            After experiencing precipitation ... the flight said they were going to climb.
      
    
            Then in a mayday call ... the flight crew alerted air traffic control that they were descending 10,000 feet per minute.
      
    
            The call then became more frantic ... as the crew shared that they were now descending 20,000 feet per minute. Flight data would eventually show them descending 32,000 feet per minute -- roughly 360 MPH.
      
    
            Eventually, the crew member tells air traffic controllers ... "We're going to crash into the ground."
      
    
            After the crew member let out a high pitch scream, the air traffic controller then responded ... "I'm here with you, talk with me."
      
    
            The crew member then responded that the aircraft was banking at 60 degrees ... before their audio cut out.
      
    
            We reported earlier ... all 9 people aboard died after the plane crashed near the Cresthaven neighborhood close to Greenacres, Florida, just miles away from Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago.
